content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I read the paper at least twice and used my best judgement in assessing the paper.
content.review:
In this work, the authors tackle the problem of building dialogue systems that can handle diverse domains and exhibit both chit-chat as well as goal-oriented behavior. The authors describe these different functionalities as different skills. Their work proposes a dialogue model inspired by the Mixture of Experts architecture (Jacobs et. al.), which learns different skills through distinct parameters which are then mixed together in a soft fashion through learned weights. On a combined dataset consisting of MultiWOZ (Budzianowski et. al.), In-Car Assistant (Eric et. al.), and the Persona Chat (Zhang et. al.), the proposed Attention Over Parameters (AoP) model outperforms other baselines on F1, BLEU, SQL query accuracy, and Booking statement accuracy. On a Persona chat evaluation, the AoP also outperforms baselines on a consistency metric calculated via a natural language inference scoring model trained from a dialogue NLI corpus (Sean et. al.)

While the problem the authors were tackling is an important one (namely combining chit-chat and goal-oriented dialogue systems), I had several problems with the proposed approach. First off, it is still not clear to me how different the AoP model truly is from a mixture-of-experts model, and in particular the differences presented in Figure 1 are not well-explained. 

Moreover, the AoP model does not seem like a novel or significant enough contribution. From my understanding, it simply feels like trying to learn separate decoders per skill and then just softly combining them through an attention weight. Why is having explicit decoders strictly necessary, rather than playing with the multiheads of the self-attention operation?

In addition, I had issues with the evaluation presented. While the model seemed to outperform some simplistic baselines (transformer and seq2seq architectures) on automatic evaluation, there was no human evaluation done. It is difficult to assess how good the generated outputs are from automatic evaluation alone. 

Finally, the authors claim that the model learns fine-grained skill decomposition, and they demonstrate this by fixing their attention weights and showing that they can generate very different output sequences. The only example of this claim is a (potentially) cherry-picked example, and without any larger scale quantitative analysis (with some sort of human eval), it is difficult to know whether the model is actually learning skill decomposition in its separate decoders.

content.title: RE: Reviewer 3
content.comment:
Thanks for your comments, let us clarify some points:

- The main differences between AoP and MoE are:
       - The MoE proposed by N Shazeer 2017, added some linear layer in between of two LSTM layers (decoders), where 
         instead we use the entire transformer decoder, even though our description is general for any type of model.
       - The major difference is that we mix the parameters before the forward pass, which is both novel and 
          computationally more efficient (Appendix Proof 1). 

-To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to propose a different parametrization for different dialogue “skills” in task-oriented and chit-chat model. Notice that in our implementation we use the whole parameter of the decoder, which includes the linear transformation of the multi-head attention. Thus, we could restrict the mix just at that level. We will include these experiments in the coming version of the paper.

- As we also mention in the reviewer 1 in n task-oriented dialogue systems, thus for both multiWOZ and SMD dataset, human evaluation is strongly correlated to automatic measures since by F1-score (Table 2) measures the ability to predict correct and inform entities and the BLUE score measure the response overlap with the gold response. Other existing paper, indeed shown that this measure correlates with human judgement especially in this datasets (Wu. et. al.ICLR 2019). On the other hand, chit-chat requires human evaluation. In this article, we did not report this number since all the baselines had a similar automatic score, which is in line with existing paper (Zhang et. al. ACL 2018, Persona-Chat), and thus already human evaluated. 
 
- We fully agree, but we could not report more example due to limited space. We will release a plain text file with the many more examples where the same behaviour holds. This is more a good inductive bias in the model and it has been verified by qualitative studies.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
1. Summary: The authors of this paper proposed an attention over parameters based model for dialogue response generation. They assume that different tasks or topics require different models to generate responses. To model this idea, they design a model that can generate an attention vector based on historical dialogue history. This attention vector can then be used to get a combination of parameters that focus on the right topic/task to generate the next response.
2. Overall assessment: This idea looks very interesting to me. It's simple but effective. However, this paper can still be improved in several aspects and it is not qualified yet to be published in a very competitive conference such as ICLR. I hope the authors can keep improving this paper and makes it a stronger publication.
3. Comments:
3.1 It seems not necessary to model the whole dialogue history. The next response usually mostly depends on the most recent user queries. Meanwhile, with a long sequence of words to encode, the model may not be very efficient. How well does the model work if only a subset of the dialogue history, such as the most recent one or two rounds, is modeled?
3.2 Before formula (2), $Y_{:k-1} = \{<SOS>, y_1, \cdots, y_k \}$, is it $y_k$ or $y_{k-1}$?
3.3 How do the authors combine the three training datasets? This is very important information for other researchers to replicate this work.
3.4 How to get the prior knowledge vector? It is given in the training data? What if we need to work on a dataset without such information? Will the model still work well? What if we remove the supervision over the attention vector in formula (8)? I suggest the authors conduct some experiments and analysis to answer these questions.
3.5 From an engineering angle, how efficient is it to derive different decoder parameters for different instances and do the inference? As we know, having constant parameters at inference time enables us to do a lot of optimization and parallelizations.  How is the efficiency of the proposed model compared with existing ones?

content.title: RE: Reviewer 2
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments, let us clarify some of the points you made:

3.1  MultiWOZ 2 (Budzianowski et. al. EMNLP 2018) has been designed to use multiple turns for generating the correct answers, thus we included the whole dialogue history in the model’s input. In some cases, like in persona-chat, there could be cases where just two turns are sufficient, but in general, the whole dialogue should be kept. 

3.2 that was a typo thank you for pointing it out. We will correct it in the next version.

3.3 Due to limited space in the main article we added information related to the dataset pre-processing in the Appendix. Notice that all three datasets are pairs input-output, thus we simply combined them. Figure 1 shows a real example from the dataset, we kept all real entity and output from the SQL queries (table of data).

3.4 The prior knowledge vector is provided by the different domains in the datasets (e.g. restaurant, hotel, persona chat etc.), and by the response that requires SQL queries (e.g. SQL and BOOK). This information is usually given in task-oriented dialogue and they are less expensive to annotate compare to Speech acts, which is usually needed in traditional modularized dialogue systems. 
What if we remove the supervision over the attention vector in formula (8)? 
This experiment is reported in the penultimate row of Table 2 (AoP w/o LV), and we discuss it in the experiment section.

3.5. For the current AoP implementation, the code static models (Seq2Seq and Transformer) are faster since no parameter mixing is required. AoP could be highly parallelizable, by precomputing the combination of parameters and by selecting the static one when needed. Moreover, AoP is faster than the original Mixture-of-Expert, proof in the Appendix.

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
The basic idea of this paper is to relate attention over parameters for different possible dialogue skills, so as to compose different sets of skills. It is an interesting idea but the paper lacks motivation and clarity on the technical content. Too implementation details are discussed, making it hard to grasp the basic ideas and motivation for the work.

I didn't understand the clear motivation for the problem setting considered in this paper. Why combine three datasets? What is real world scenario where it is desired to do both task oriented dialog and chit chat together? Are we arguing that dialog dataset from chit chat can help learn task driven dialogues and vice versa?

Some of the baseline models considered in the paper are not really dialog models but neural networks employed in the proposed dialog modeling setting.

I would like to see human evaluation for any dialog model. Otherwise, we are throwing arrows in the dark.

I didn't understand a clear motivation for using SQL queries, and authors emphasize upon it at multiple places.

content.title: RE: Reviewer 1
content.comment:
Thanks for your insightful comments, let us clarify some points:

- The motivation to build a single model that is able to accomplish both tasks, chit-chat and task-oriented is to allowed the users to freely interact with the dialogue model. For instance, all the recent dialogue assistant (Siri, Alexa etc.) are both task-oriented and chit-chat. However, the current technology relies on modularized/rule-based systems, where, instead, in this paper, we proposed a single end-to-end model. This leads us to build a single dataset (by joining three datasets) that requires multiple dialogue ability. At the current stage, we could not make a strong argument that chit-chat and task-oriented help each other, but from the reported results they do not hurt each other, which is not always the case for multi-task learning. 

- Seq2seq and Transformer are de-facto baselines for conversational models. Indeed, one of the first-ever propose Seq2Seq models was  (A Neural Conversational Model, Vinyals et. al. JMLR 2015) used for modelling conversations. Seq2Seq and Transformer showed great potential in modelling conversations, for example, the two winning models of the ConvAI challenge held in NIPS last year, was win by Transformer models (GPT2 finetuning).
In task-oriented dialogue systems, thus for both multiWOZ and SMD dataset, human evaluation is strongly correlated to automatic measures since by F1-score (Table 2) measures the ability to predict correct and inform entities and the BLUE score measure the response overlap with the gold response. Other existing paper, indeed shown that this measure correlate with human judgement especially in this datasets (Wu. et. al.ICLR 2019). 
On the other hand, chit-chat requires human evaluation. In this article, we did not report this number since all the baselines had a similar automatic score, which are in line with existing paper (Zhang et. al. ACL 2018, Persona-Chat), and thus already human evaluated. 

- SQL query is used to retrieve knowledge from the ontology, and to query the booking system. Previous works in end-to-end dialogue (Bordes et. al. ICLR 2017) used simpler grammars like (API_CALL Att_1 Att_2 Att_3) but the provided ontology was simpler. Notice that the dataset has been pre-processed for the end-to-end training, thus SQL query has been added — just when needed-- using the dialogue state. Connecting with the previous point, the evaluation of the SQL generation has been also reported in both table 2 and the appendix (by domain).
